doc.title: Fred Radke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Hillsdale, Michigan, November 8, 2023

title: Wanting to be a trumpet player; Welldonians youth band in Oakland
summary: Radke decided on trumpet after seeing Harry James on TV at about seven, got a school cornet, and joined the strict 250-piece Welldonians marching band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and I’m here at beautiful Hillsdale College with Fred Radke, and I’m very pleased to meet you. And you’ve already enthralled me with some stories so you’re just going to have to tell them all again.
Oh, I don’t know about that.
I wanted to ask you, when in your youth did you decide that you wanted to be a professional musician?
Well I wanted to be a trumpet player, that was the first thing I wanted to be. Period.

Anything. Yeah. I was, I don’t know, about six or — about seven — and I saw Harry James on television. And I said, “That’s what I want to play, and that’s what I want to do.” So grammar school — you were supposed to be a year older to get a horn but we talked to the teacher and I got a horn from the school, some beat-up old Buescher cornet you know. And I wanted to play. And I started playing and playing in the school band. And then in Oakland, I grew up in Oakland, California, that’s my hometown. And there was a famous youth band there called The Welldonians. And it was a 250 piece marching band. And it was very dedicated young musicians from the age of two to eighteen. And outstanding, the older trumpet players were really good you know, that later on became known players. But it was a very militaristic organization, very disciplined. Finally when you learned your parade routine and let’s say you played third trumpet, you had to audition in front of three officers in order to get your parade uniform, your cape and cap. And you had to do the 15-minute routine, marching steps, and you’re playing third — with nothing else around you — and you were allowed to make zero mistakes. You made one mistake you didn’t get the thing, and come back in two weeks.
Would that include the marching part of it?

Oh absolutely. This was an incredible — when this unit marched down the street — now all these big bands, school bands, are something. But this was one of the first ones like that.
